title: A solid of revolution with cut-away: what does it look like inside?
summary: A 3D view of a solid made by spinning a profile about an axis, with a quarter removed so the interior shows. The profile curve, the axis and the cut planes are marked in different colours.

media.alt: A translucent teal 3D solid of revolution along the x axis, wider at the right end, with a quarter wedge cut out showing two orange flat faces. A blue profile curve, a rose axis line, a legend and a note about the removed quarter.
media.caption: Reference render of class F3.5 (design-system gallery). The data are synthetic and exist only to demonstrate the form.

source.note: Plot class from the design system's plot taxonomy; synthetic demonstration data. Standard theory only.

read_the_figure.question: What does it look like inside?
read_the_figure.axes: Three axes x, y, z with x along the solid's axis (0 to 2, drawn longer by the box aspect 2.4 : 1 : 1), y and z from -1.3 to 1.3. Teal surface: the outside. Amber planes: the cut faces at y = 0 and z = 0. Blue: the profile curve r(x). Rose: the axis of revolution.
look_at: Where is the axis (rose) and where is the profile curve (blue)?
Are the cut faces the amber planes through the axis?
Where is the solid narrowest and widest?
How much of the solid was removed?
as_drawn: The profile is r(x) = 0.5 + 0.35 sin^2(2.2x) + 0.15x on [0, 2]: 0.5 at the left, 1.12 at the right, with a neck near x = 1.4 (r about 0.71).
A quarter wedge (angle from 0 to 90 degrees) is removed, so 3/4 of the solid remains: V = 4.29 for the full solid, 3.22 for the cut-away.
The picture is hard to read: the translucent surface mixes with the cut faces and the profile line sits on the surface, so depth is ambiguous. This is a known weakness of 3D renders.
read_the_figure.proves: The qualitative shape of the solid and how the profile maps to the surface. It cannot be used to read off radii or volumes: perspective, transparency and shading distort them.
if_wrong: No axis drawn: you cannot tell what the surface rotates about.
No cut or section: the interior is hidden.
Heavy transparency with no ordering: layers blend into one colour.

terms.meaning: The 2D curve that is spun to make the solid.
The line about which the profile is spun.
A removed part of the solid that exposes the interior.
The flat surface where the solid has been sliced.
The effect that nearer parts look bigger on a 2D screen.
The solid's volume, pi times the integral of r squared along the axis.

remember: A solid of revolution has circular cross-sections about the axis.
Draw the axis and the profile in distinct colours.
Cut away a wedge to show the interior; state the fraction removed.
Do not read lengths off a 3D perspective view.

understand.title: Marks and encodings
understand.text: The translucent teal surface is the outside; opaque-looking amber faces are the cuts; a blue line is the profile (the generator); a thick rose line is the axis. Position is in three-dimensional space, shown by a fixed viewing angle (elevation 24, azimuth -58).

understand.title: Why this form answers the question
understand.text: An unfamiliar 3D shape is easier to understand when you can see the 2D profile that makes it and the axis it turns about. The cut-away shows that the cross-sections are full disks (the interior is solid). The picture ties the abstract formula (rotate r(x) about x) to a shape.

understand.title: How it misleads
understand.text: In perspective, the right-hand end looks bigger partly because it is nearer. Transparency hides depth order and mixes the colours of surface and faces. The box aspect (2.4 : 1 : 1) changes proportions. A single viewpoint leaves out what is behind. The fraction removed can only be read from the note.

understand.title: Why each required item matters
understand.text: The marked axis tells you what the surface is a revolution about. The cut-away plane shows the interior, which a closed surface would hide. A note stating the quarter removed fixes the remaining volume; without it the cut-away could be any fraction.

understand.title: Alternatives
understand.text: For measurements use a 2D slice view with A(x) (F3.3). For an overview use several orthographic views. For the interior structure an interactive rotatable view is the best choice. For a quick numeric check use the formula V = pi integral r^2 dx.

understand.title: A variant to create
understand.text: Draw the cut at three different wedge angles, shade the cut face in opaque amber, and add a small inset showing the profile with the axis.

steps.title: Volume of the solid and of the cut-away
steps.note: For r(x) = 0.5 + 0.35 sin^2(2.2x) + 0.15x. Removing a quarter wedge removes exactly one quarter of every disk, hence one quarter of the volume.

steps.title: Where the neck is
steps.note: Between the two humps the sine-squared term vanishes at x = 1.43, leaving only the linear growth term. The true minimum of r is a little to the left, at x = 1.38 with r = 0.711, so the neck is at about 1.4 with r about 0.71.

worked.title: Reading the reference render
worked.problem: From the figure and the stated formula: (1) which end is wider and by how much? (2) Where is the neck? (3) What fraction of the solid is shown?

solution.text: The right end (x = 2) is wider: r = 0.5 + 0.35 sin^2(4.4) + 0.30 = 1.12, against 0.5 at the left end.
Near x = 1.4, where the sine-squared term vanishes (x = 1.43), r = 0.71.
Three quarters: a quarter wedge is removed, as the footnote says.

worked.answer: The right end is more than twice as wide as the left; the neck is near x = 1.4 with r about 0.71; the picture shows 3/4 of the solid.

create: Draw the same solid with an opaque cut face and no transparency.
Add three coloured cross-section circles at x = 0.5, 1.0, 1.5 with their areas printed.

checks.q: What shape are the cross-sections of a solid of revolution perpendicular to its axis?
A quarter wedge is removed from a solid of volume 4.29. What volume remains?
Why is it unwise to measure the radius from a perspective 3D plot?
checks.answer: Perspective makes nearer parts look larger and the plot's box aspect changes proportions; use a 2D section or numbers.
